steps.label: Conclusion (prediction = opinion)
steps.body: Widespread use of encryption software will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
steps.body: The most interesting, revealing source material for a biography will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Public figures' private correspondence and diaries are meant to be confidential when written, but they later become biographers' principal sources. In the future, most such documents are likely to be stored as encrypted text, which can be opened by password only.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, read with one expectation in mind: the conclusion usually arrives before its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or the sentence right after a pivot like "however."

So test the first sentence. It is a prediction: encryption "will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end." Nobody can observe the future, so a prediction is an opinion, and an opinion needs support. Ask: why should we believe that? The rest of the paragraph answers. Diaries and letters are the biographers' main sources. Those documents will likely be encrypted. So historians without passwords will lose the best material. Every later sentence is a reason for the first one.

Notice the chain has two levels. The "so" claim (historians will lose the revealing material) is itself a conclusion, supported by the encryption premise. But the argument does not stop there. Losing that material matters because it ends biographical writing. When one conclusion supports another, the one that supports nothing further is the main conclusion.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Find a meaning match for the first sentence: widespread encryption will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end. "Virtually to an end" means almost stopping, so a matching answer can say it will nearly stop, sharply decline, or cease.

Expect traps that restate the encryption premise or the "so" claim about historians losing access. Both sit on the path to the conclusion, but neither is where the argument ends up.

notes.body: This is the premise about storage: "most such documents are likely to be stored as encrypted text." Run the support test. Why does the author think biography will end? Partly because of this. A reason offered for the conclusion is evidence, not the conclusion. A also hardens "likely" into "will be."

This matches the first sentence piece by piece. "widespread use of encryption software" carries over unchanged. "will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end" becomes "will cause the writing of biographical history to decline significantly or cease." An almost-end is a significant decline, and an actual end is ceasing, so B covers the author's prediction without adding or dropping anything.

The move to repeat: once you have located the conclusion, put it in plainer words and look for the answer that says the same thing. On Main Conclusion, the correct answer is usually a paraphrase of one sentence, not a new idea.

This is close to the "so" claim: without passwords, historians lose the most revealing material. That claim is supported by the encryption premise, and it in turn supports the first sentence. Ask what it is for. Historians losing access is the reason biography will end. A claim that supports something else in the paragraph is not the main conclusion.

This is the last-claim trap. D restates the final sentence: the most interesting, revealing material "will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords." It feels like the conclusion because it follows "so," and it is a conclusion, but only an intermediate one.

Run the support test in both directions. Why should we believe biography will end? Because historians will lose the best material without passwords. Why should we believe historians will lose it? Because the documents will be encrypted. The password claim sits in the middle of that chain. The first sentence is the only claim that is supported and supports nothing further, so it is the main conclusion.

The stimulus calls these documents biographers' "principal sources" and implies the most revealing material sits in them. E turns that into a ranking of all sources, which the author never states. Even as an implied idea, it would be background that explains why losing the documents matters. It supports the prediction; it is not the prediction.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes, 100+ word repetitive notes, 'She' for the author in Evaluate, a one-line Goal, and an Evidence step that drifted from the stimulus wording.

steps.label: Conclusion (clearly = opinion)
steps.body: Radioactive elements are still being created in the universe today (whether or not some of them were also created when the universe began).

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
steps.body: If no new radioactive elements had been created after the universe began, almost no radioactive elements would be left in the universe today.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Radioactive elements are unstable, so most of them decay within at most a few million years into other, nonradioactive elements. Yet there is an abundance of radioactive elements in the universe today.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before its support. It is usually the first sentence or the sentence after a pivot.

The first sentence hedges: radioactive elements "may have been created when the universe began." A "may" claim is a concession, not something the author sets out to prove. Then the pivot: "However, even if this occurred, these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." "Clearly" marks the author's own view. Check it with the support test: why should we believe new radioactive elements are being created?

The rest of the paragraph answers that question. Most radioactive elements decay within a few million years. So if none had been made since the beginning, almost none would be left. But there are plenty left. Lined up:

No new elements created after the beginning → almost none left today
Not almost none left (there is an abundance)
So: new elements have been created

That is the contrapositive at work, and it lands exactly on the second sentence.

The final sentence starts with "So," which tempts us to call it the conclusion. It is a conclusion, but an intermediate one: it is drawn from the decay premise and then used to prove the second sentence. On Main Conclusion, the last sentence is rarely the answer, so check it before you trust it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a meaning match for the second sentence: "these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." Swap the pronoun for what it refers to: radioactive elements are still being created today. The answer does not need "clearly" or the "even if" clause.

Expect traps built from the "So" sentence, the decay premise, and the opening concession.

notes.body: The argument never states this. It is an inference you might draw from the decay premise, but a Main Conclusion answer has to restate the claim the author argues for. A is also about the wrong subject: the author's point is that new elements are being made today, not what became of the original ones.

This is the second sentence with the pronoun swapped out. "these elements" means radioactive elements, and "are clearly still being created in the universe today" becomes "are being created in the universe today." Dropping "clearly" and "still" does not change the claim.

Confirm with the support test. Everything else in the paragraph (the decay rate, the conditional, the abundance) answers one question: why believe new radioactive elements are being made? When a sentence after a pivot is backed by everything that follows, you have found the main conclusion.

This is the final sentence's conditional, and the "So" in front of it is the bait. It is a conclusion, drawn from the premise that most radioactive elements decay within a few million years. But the argument does not stop there. The author pairs it with the abundance of radioactive elements to prove something else: new ones must be forming. A claim that is supported and then used as support is an intermediate conclusion. When the last sentence opens with "so," ask whether it is used to prove anything further before you pick it.

This is the opening concession. "may have been created" is a possibility the author grants and then sets aside with "even if this occurred." Nothing in the paragraph argues for it. A claim the author concedes and moves past is background, not the conclusion.

This restates the third sentence: instability plus the decay timeline. It is the first link in the chain. Because the elements decay so fast, almost none would be left without new creation. The author offers it to prove something else, so it is support, not the point being supported.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes, repetitive 100+ word notes; Evidence step dropped 'most' from the decay premise; Evaluate had flattened bullets and garbled phrasing ('no new radioactive were being created'); Goal misquoted the conclusion sentence.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It's a mistake to assume figuring out what caused the recession is essential to improving the economy.

steps.label: Evidence (after all)
steps.body: Corrective lenses were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion to come before at least some of its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.

This one is the rebuttal. The first sentence is a fact: people are debating what caused the recession. Nothing supports it, and nothing needs to. Then the pivot: "It is a mistake, however, to assume..." That is the columnist taking a side.

To confirm, run the support test: why should we believe that answering the cause question is not essential? The next sentence opens with "after all," a support indicator, and gives a reason. Corrective lenses treated myopia well before anyone knew the cause was genetic. So a problem can be treated without knowing its cause.

The four support indicators to listen for are for, after all, because, and since (FABS). When one of them opens a sentence, the claim right before it is usually what it supports.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
When we have rebuttal-style conclusions, take an extra second to state the author's position in the words of the position being rebutted. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they're wrong," then the conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable."

Here the opposing position is: "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It's essential." The columnist says that is a mistake. It's not essential. You could improve the economy even if you never figured out what caused the recession.

Notice what kind of claim that is. "Essential" means required, so the columnist is saying knowing the cause is not necessary for improvement. Find the answer that says knowing the cause is not required, and nothing stronger.

notes.body: The columnist talks about one problem: the current recession. A turns that into a rule for every problem, and "never" makes it absolute. One myopia example can show that some fixes work without knowing the cause. It cannot show that no problem ever requires finding the cause.

B swaps necessary for sufficient. The columnist says knowing the cause is not essential: you can improve the economy without it. B says knowing the cause "would not necessarily enable people to find a solution": knowing it might not be enough. Those are different claims.

Test it. Imagine knowing the cause always led straight to a fix. B would be false, yet the columnist's point would survive, because the economy could still be improved without that knowledge. When a conclusion says something is not required, check that the answer is not really about whether it is enough.

This is the opening fact that sets up the debate. The columnist offers no reason to believe the question is hotly debated, and the rest of the paragraph does not try to prove it. A claim that nothing supports and that only introduces the topic is background, not the conclusion.

This is the second sentence translated. The columnist says it is "a mistake" to assume that answering the cause question "is essential to improving the economy." D says the same thing with "need not": you can improve the economy without ascertaining the cause of the recession.

The move to repeat: when the conclusion rejects someone else's view, restate it as the denial of that view (essential becomes not needed), then match. D also keeps the scope to the current recession, which is what keeps it from overreaching the way A does.

This is the evidence, introduced by "after all." The myopia example is the reason the columnist gives for the claim about the recession. Ask which claim it is offered to prove: that knowing a cause is not essential to a fix. Support for the conclusion cannot be the conclusion.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes and repetitive 100+ word notes; Goal used 'she' for the columnist; Evaluate had flattened bullets; the correct note never showed the word-level match.

steps.label: Conclusion (this means that)
steps.body: We can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Railroads rely increasingly on automation. Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced. The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck, and no reduction in operating costs is predicted for the trucking industry.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before at least some of the evidence. Usually it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.

This one breaks the usual pattern. The first sentence is a plain fact about automation, and nothing argues for it. The second sentence is a claim about costs, supported by the worker reduction ("Since fewer railroad workers are needed"). The third sentence is the first one that sounds like the author looking ahead: "This means that we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow." "We can expect" is a prediction, and "This means that" tells us it is drawn from what came before.

Run the support test. Why should we believe rail freight will grow? Because rail's costs went down. Then the last sentence adds a second reason after the conclusion: trucking, the main competitor, is not getting cheaper. So the conclusion sits in the middle, with support on both sides.

Phrases like "this means that," "this shows that," and "this suggests that" can mark a main conclusion just as well as "therefore." Don't assume the conclusion has to be the first or last sentence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find the answer that matches the third sentence: rail freight volume is expected to grow. Watch for answers that restate the cost claim or the trucking premise. They are reasons for the prediction, not the prediction.

notes.body: This is the third sentence nearly word for word. "we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow" becomes "can be expected to increase." Confirm with the support test. Lower rail costs and flat trucking costs are both reasons to expect more freight on rail, and the freight claim is not used to prove anything else. When a claim is supported from both sides and supports nothing further, it is the main conclusion, wherever it sits.

This links the first two sentences: automation means fewer workers. The stimulus treats that link as a starting point and uses the worker reduction to explain the lower operating costs. Ask what it is for: it feeds the cost claim, which feeds the freight prediction. A claim that only feeds the chain is not the conclusion.

This is the last sentence, and it is a premise. The author uses it to show that rail's cost advantage is real: trucks are not getting cheaper too. It gives a reason to expect rail freight to grow, so it supports the conclusion rather than being it. Don't pick the final claim just because it comes last.

This is the strongest decoy because it is supported. "Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced" gives a reason for the cost claim, so the cost claim is a conclusion of sorts. But the author does not stop there. "This means that" takes the lower costs and draws a further claim from them: freight volume will grow. The cost reduction is supported and then used as support, which makes it an intermediate conclusion. The main conclusion is the claim at the end of that chain.

This is background from the last sentence. It names the competitor so the cost comparison means something. Nothing in the paragraph argues that trucking is rail's chief competitor; the author states it and uses it. An unsupported fact that feeds the argument is a premise, not the conclusion.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes and boilerplate notes; B's note wrongly called 'automation means fewer workers' an intermediate conclusion supported in the stimulus; Evaluate overstated that Main Conclusion never uses 'therefore'-type indicators; Goal was filler.

steps.label: Conclusion (not justified = opinion)
steps.body: The conclusion that ocean warming is a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution is far from justified.

steps.label: Evidence (it is known that)
steps.body: There are many natural cycles of ocean temperature changes that last 60 years or more.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that 90% of the time, the conclusion will be the first sentence or it will be a rebuttal.
In this argument, the first sentence is clearly factual, not the author's opinion, so it's not a First Sentence Conclusion.
And when the second sentence begins with an attribution, "Some scientists claim", we would anticipate a Pivot into a Rebuttal.
Sure enough, we get "However, this conclusion is far from justified". The last sentence provides factual support. We can tell the last claim is factual because it is prefaced by "it is known that".

Confirm with the support test: why should we believe the scientists' conclusion is far from justified? Because natural cycles of ocean temperature can last 60 years or more, so a 15-year warming trend could be part of one. That is a reason to doubt the scientists' explanation, not proof that it is false. So the climatologist's conclusion is about the evidence: the human-pollution explanation has not been established.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Since our conclusion has a pronoun, "this conclusion is far from justified", we should take a sec and insert in the specific language the pronoun is referring to, as we did above when we wrote the Conclusion.
We should also limber up our synonym faculties by thinking, "What's another way to say this conclusion is far from justified?" Saying it's incorrect is too strong. It's more like "it's hasty to draw this conclusion / it's prematurely inferred / we don't have strong evidence for this".

notes.body: The climatologist states the 4-degree warming as a fact and does not argue for it. A also changes the claim: the stimulus never says some scientists found this evidence, and it never calls the warming "significant." The warming is the starting fact; the argument is about what explains it.

B is tempting because it points the same direction as the climatologist. But B says the warming is not a symptom of global warming. The climatologist only says that conclusion is "far from justified." Not proven is weaker than false. Natural cycles show the warming might be natural; they do not show it is.

Test it: could the climatologist accept that the warming really is caused by pollution, while still holding that the scientists have not yet justified saying so? Yes. So B overstates the conclusion. On Main Conclusion, match the author's strength, not just the author's side.

This is the rebuttal sentence with the pronoun filled in. "this conclusion" refers to the scientists' claim that the warming is a symptom of global warming caused by human-generated air pollution. C spells that out and keeps "is far from justified." Everything else in the paragraph serves that judgment: the warming is the scientists' starting fact, and the natural cycles are the climatologist's reason.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion contains "this" or "that," fill in what it points to, then look for the answer that keeps the author's exact strength. Here that strength is "not justified," not "false."

D says what the natural-cycle evidence suggests: the warming might be natural. The climatologist never says this outright, and even as an implied step it plays a supporting role. It is why the pollution explanation is far from justified. Support for the conclusion is not the conclusion.

This conditional never appears in the stimulus. It also adds a claim the climatologist does not need: that a natural cycle and human-caused global warming could not both be at work. The climatologist's point is about the evidence, that the pollution explanation is not justified, not a rule about which causes exclude each other.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes and 100 to 150 word notes repeating 'building blocks' and 'edifice'; Evaluate said 'first case' for first sentence and never ran the support test; notes did not tie each trap to its own wording.

steps.label: Rossi's Argument
steps.body: Rossi states a general principle ("It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented") and applies it to children: since children's interests are sometimes different from their parents', children should have the right to vote.

steps.label: Smith's response (background)
steps.body: Smith concedes Rossi's point about different interests but raises a separate practical objection: children's conceptions and time horizons are too immature for voting responsibility.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The stem asks only about Rossi, so Smith's reply is background here. Read Rossi's two sentences as conclusion plus evidence.

Conclusion: children should have the right to vote.
Evidence: it is undemocratic for people to live under a government that does not represent their interests, and children's interests are sometimes different from their parents'.

Now characterize the evidence. The first sentence is not about children at all. It is a broad rule about all people: if your interests are not represented, your situation is undemocratic. The second sentence plugs children into that rule. Their interests can differ from their parents', so the parents' votes do not fully represent them, so by the rule children need a vote of their own.

That is one of the standard Method moves: state a general principle, then apply it to a specific case. Other common moves are analogy, counterexample, ruling out alternatives, and raising an overlooked consideration. None of those fits Rossi. There is no comparison case, no exception, and no rival explanation.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying Rossi relies on a general principle, or applies a broad rule to a specific group. Check every answer against Rossi's argument only. Smith's reasoning is the source of at least one trap.

notes.body:
Rossi's first sentence is a general rule: it is undemocratic for anyone to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Rossi then applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so, by the rule, children need their own representation, which means the vote.

"Appeal to a general principle" is how the LSAT describes this move. When an argument opens with a broad "it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ..." claim and then applies it to a specific case, look for this answer.

Rossi speaks first, so there is no opponent yet, and Rossi never questions anyone's honesty or motives. Smith doesn't either: Smith grants Rossi's point about interests and disagrees on the merits. An answer about bad faith needs an accusation in the text, and there is none.

Rossi's argument is about what is democratic, not about what would happen if children voted. Rossi never predicts a single result. Smith's worry that children's conceptions are too simple comes closer to practical concerns, which is why C can feel familiar: it fits the other speaker better.

D can tempt because Rossi's argument is short and sounds like a pair of statements. But Rossi does give a rationale. The policy is "children should have the right to vote." The rationale is the principle (living with unrepresented interests is undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ from their parents'). Test it: ask Rossi "why should children vote?" Rossi has an answer. An argument that substituted description for a rationale would only describe children or voting and never say why the policy follows.

This describes equivocation: one word used in two senses. The only term Rossi repeats is "interests," and it means the same thing both times: what is good for a person or group. With no shift in meaning, there is no equivocation.

why: Notes now exist (known_problem is stale) but use 'he' for Rossi throughout, the D and B notes lean on unverified popularity claims or a bare verdict, and the Evaluate and Goal steps were one-line restatements.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: You can rely on Barr Motor Company to produce more winning automobiles than its competitors.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: (1) The pride at Austin Stables accounts for their success in producing more winning racehorses than any other stable. (2) For generations, Barr Motor Company has demonstrated similar pride. (3) That tradition of pride is not limited to horse racing.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The ad's structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.

The sentence "Such a tradition of pride is not only found in the business of horse racing" is the bridge. It tells us the ad wants pride's payoff in one business to carry over to another. That is how an analogy works: what is true of one case is claimed for a similar case.

On Method, run the "argues X by Y" test on every answer: X has to match the conclusion and Y has to match the evidence. Here X is that Barr will beat its competitors, and Y is a comparison to a stable whose pride made it a winner. An answer that gets either half wrong is out.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find an answer that describes the analogy-to-conclusion structure: an analogy is used to support a conclusion that Barr is superior to its competitors.

notes.body: The ad never mentions customers, repeat or otherwise. Its only evidence is pride and winning. A Method answer has to describe what the argument actually does, and nothing in the ad demonstrates anything about who comes back to buy.

Check both halves. Conclusion: "superior to its competitors" matches "produce more winning automobiles than our competitors." Evidence: "using an analogy" matches the Austin Stables comparison. Pride made Austin beat other stables; Barr has similar pride; so Barr will beat other car makers.

When an argument borrows a result from one situation and claims it for a similar one, expect the Method answer to say analogy.

C names something the ad does say: Barr has shown pride "For generations." But the ad only asserts it; nothing in the ad proves it. And it is a premise, not where the ad is going. The ad's point is that Barr will out-win its competitors. Asserting a premise and proving a claim are different moves, and a Method answer has to describe the argument's actual work.

The ad credits pride fully: pride "accounts for" Austin's success. It plays pride's role up, not down. Understating it would undercut the ad's own analogy, since Barr's case rests on pride being what makes the difference.

The ad never compares the ages of the two traditions. It says Barr has shown pride "For generations" and calls Austin's pride a tradition, but it never says which is older. The analogy needs the pride to be similar, not older.

why: Notes now exist (known_problem is stale) but are one-line verdicts (A, E), the correct note never ran the conclusion/evidence match, and C claimed unverified popularity; Evaluate lacked the 'argues X by Y' test.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Pointing out that the correlation (people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract rather than physical concepts) is far from universal is not enough reason to reject the researchers' claim.

steps.label: Evidence (because)
steps.body: Some people perceive words like "comprehension" as expressing a physical action, like grasping something, rather than a state of understanding, which is abstract.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with what the author is responding to. Researchers say people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract concepts. A critic could point out exceptions: people who gesture while discussing something abstract. The author says exceptions like that are not enough to throw out the claim.

Why not? Because some of the exceptions may not be exceptions at all. Take someone who gestures while talking about comprehension. That looks like a strike against the researchers, since comprehension, as a state of understanding, is abstract. But if that person thinks of comprehension as grasping something, a physical action, then the person is talking about a physical concept, and gesturing is exactly what the researchers' claim predicts.

So the author keeps the generalization and explains away the counterevidence. The cases that seem to break the pattern are reclassified using a fact about how people perceive words. Notice that the author never says the correlation is universal and never brings in new support for it. The job is defensive: show that the apparent exceptions do not hurt the claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Use "argues X by Y" on every answer. X should match the conclusion: the researchers' claim survives the objection that the correlation is far from universal. Y should match the evidence: a fact about how some people perceive certain words.

In Method terms, the author answers a counterexample by giving it an alternate explanation that fits the rule. So look for something like: "uses a fact about how people perceive words to show that apparent exceptions are consistent with the generalization."

notes.body: A is tempting because the evidence really does turn on a word with two readings: comprehension as grasping or as understanding. But check the X half. The author does not try to show the correlation is universal. The argument never disputes that it is "far from universal" and claims only that this is "insufficient reason to reject the researchers’ claim." A tendency can hold without being universal. An answer that gets the goal of the argument wrong fails even when its method half sounds right.

The fact the author cites is about "some people," not everyone, so it is not a universal generalization. And it is not offered as fresh support for a claim about gestures. It is offered to explain why certain exceptions do not count against the researchers' claim.

Match it piece by piece. "citing a psychological fact": some people perceive "comprehension" as a physical action. "a generalization": people tend to gesture less with abstract concepts. "apparently disconfirming evidence": cases where the correlation seems to fail. "reconcile": show those cases fit after all, because the speaker treats the concept as physical.

The move to repeat: when an author defends a rule against exceptions by explaining why the exceptions are not what they seem, the Method answer will talk about reconciling or explaining away the counterevidence.

The author is not choosing among explanations for why people gesture. No rival explanation is named, and none is shown to be implausible. The argument defends the researchers' claim against apparent exceptions, which is a different job from eliminating alternatives.

E reverses the direction. The author argues the claim should not be rejected, not that it needs more support. E also calls the generalization "widely accepted," while the stimulus attributes it only to "Some researchers." The reason given is a reason the claim survives, not a reason to demand more evidence.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes and 100-word notes; Conclusion step overstated the claim ('does not provide any grounds'); Evaluate used a dash-style aside; Goal had a typo ('ti') and buried the prediction in a list.
